procedural_history.originating_court: Court of the Munsif, Puri; Additional Sessions Judge of Puri
procedural_history.impugned_order: Judgment and order dated March 2, 1964 of the Orissa High Court in Government Appeal No. 49 of 1963.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The State Government appealed the acquittal of the appellants by the Additional Sessions Judge to the Orissa High Court. The High Court set aside the acquittal with regard to the 4 appellants and convicted them under s. 353, Indian Penal Code. The High Court, however, held that there was no satisfactory evidence to convict the appellants under ss. 143/402, Indian Penal Code. As regards the charge under s. 186, Indian Penal Code, the High Court expressed the view that the prosecution was barred under the provisions of s. 195, Criminal Procedure Code.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The appellants appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave challenging the High Court's judgment and order dated March 2, 1964. The Supreme Court affirmed the judgment of the High Court and dismissed the appeal.

issue.issue_text: Whether the prosecution for a distinct offence under Section 353 of the Indian Penal Code is barred when it is based on the same facts as the prosecution under Section 186 of the Indian Penal Code?

facts: The appellants were charged with obstructing and assaulting public servants who were executing a court decree.
The charges included offences under Section 186 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for obstruction and Section 353 of the IPC for assault or use of criminal force.
A prosecution under Section 186 requires a written complaint from the public servant as per Section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code (CrPC), which was not filed in this case.

The appellants argued that since the prosecution for Section 186 was barred by Section 195 CrPC, the prosecution for Section 353, which was based on the same facts, should also be barred to prevent circumvention of the law.
law: Section 195 of the CrPC bars a court from taking cognizance of an offence under Section 186 IPC without a written complaint from the public servant concerned.
Section 195 of the CrPC does not mention or apply to the offence under Section 353 of the IPC.

The established legal principle is that Section 195 CrPC does not bar the trial of an accused for a distinct offence disclosed by the same set of facts, as long as that offence is not covered by Section 195.
The provisions of Section 195 CrPC cannot be evaded by using devices or camouflage, such as misdescribing an offence to avoid its requirements.
application: The Court determined that Section 186 and Section 353 of the IPC are two distinct and separate offences.
It highlighted that the ingredients of the two offences are different. Section 186 deals with mere obstruction, while Section 353 requires the specific element of 'assault or use of criminal force'.

The Court also noted that the two offences are qualitatively different, as they fall under different chapters of the IPC: Section 186 under 'Contempts of the lawful authority of public servants' and Section 353 under 'offences affecting the human body'.
Since Section 353 is a distinct offence and is not mentioned in Section 195 CrPC, the bar on taking cognizance without a written complaint does not apply to it.

The Court was satisfied that prosecuting under Section 353 was not a 'camouflage or evasion' to circumvent the requirements for a Section 186 prosecution, but was based on the distinct offence of assault disclosed by the facts.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the prosecution for the distinct offence under Section 353 of the Indian Penal Code is not barred by Section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code, even if it is based on the same facts as a prosecution under Section 186 of the Indian Penal Code.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court regarding the charge under Section 353 of the Indian Penal Code?

facts: The appellants were charged with several offences, including under Section 353 of the Indian Penal Code (IPC) for using criminal force against public servants.
The trial court (Additional Sessions Judge) acquitted the appellants of all charges.
The State Government appealed this acquittal to the High Court.
The High Court reviewed the case, set aside the trial court's acquittal regarding the charge under Section 353 IPC, and convicted the appellants for that offence.
law: An appellate court's power in an appeal against acquittal (under Section 423(1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Code) is as wide as its power in an appeal against a conviction.
The High Court has the authority to review the entire evidence on record and arrive at its own conclusion.
While doing so, the High Court must consider the reasons given by the trial court for the acquittal and must provide its own reasons for why the acquittal was not justified.

Phrases like "substantial and compelling reasons" are not a rigid formula that curtails the High Court's power, nor is it necessary for the High Court to label the trial court's findings as "perverse" before reversing an acquittal.
application: The Supreme Court tested the High Court's judgment against the established legal principles governing appeals against acquittal.
It found that the High Court had acted within its wide appellate powers by reviewing the evidence and coming to its own conclusion.
The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court's judgment was not flawed by any error of law.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court held that the High Court was justified in interfering with the trial court's order of acquittal for the charge under Section 353 of the Indian Penal Code. It found that the High Court had correctly exercised its appellate powers, and therefore, the appellants' challenge on this issue was rejected.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the prosecution for a distinct offence under Section 353 of the Indian Penal Code is barred when it is based on the same facts as the prosecution under Section 186 of the Indian Penal Code?
appellant_arguments: The prosecution under Section 353 of the Indian Penal Code was barred by Section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code.
respondent_arguments: Section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not bar the trial of an accused for a distinct offence disclosed by the same set of facts, provided it is not a camouflage to circumvent the section.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was justified in interfering with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court regarding the charge under Section 353 of the Indian Penal Code?
appellant_arguments: The High Court had no justification for interfering with the order of acquittal passed by the trial court.
The High Court did not apply the correct legal principles for reviewing an acquittal.
There was no evidence to support the High Court's finding that the appellants used criminal force against the public servants (P.Ws 1 and 2).
respondent_arguments: An appellate court has full power to review the evidence upon which an order of acquittal is founded.

The High Court correctly relied on the evidence of multiple witnesses (P.Ws 1, 2, 3, and 9 to 13) to conclude that the appellants used criminal force against the public servants while they were discharging their duties.

The High Court was justified in interfering with the acquittal, as the test of 'substantial and compelling reasons' does not curtail its power to review the entire evidence and come to its own conclusion.

cases.case_name: Sanwat Singh v. State of Rajasthan
cases.principle: An appellate court has full power to review the evidence upon which an order of acquittal is founded, and it is not necessary that before reversing an acquittal, the High Court must characterize the findings as perverse.

cases.case_name: Agarwal and Kulkarni v. State of Maharashtra
cases.principle: It is not necessary that before reversing a judgment of acquittal, the High Court must necessarily characterize the findings recorded therein as perverse.
Affords the correct guide for an appellate court's approach to a case when disposing of an appeal against an acquittal.

cases.case_name: Basir-ul-Huk v. State of West Bengal
cases.principle: Section 195, Criminal Procedure Code, does not bar the trial of an accused person for a distinct offence disclosed by the same set of facts but which is not within the ambit of that section, when there is no camouflage or evasion to circumvent the Section.

cases.case_name: Hori Ram Singh v. The Crown
cases.principle: When two distinct offences are committed in the same transaction, the fact that cognizance cannot be taken of one offence (e.g., for want of sanction) is not a bar to the trial of the other distinct offence.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: Section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not bar the trial of an accused person for a distinct offence disclosed by the same set of facts, but which is not within the ambit of that section, when there is no camouflage or evasion to circumvent the Section.
obiter: An appellate court has the full power to review the entire evidence in an appeal against an acquittal, and its power is as wide as in an appeal against a conviction.
Expressions such as 'substantial and compelling reasons' or 'strong reasons' are not intended to be a rigid formula that curtails the appellate court's power to come to its own conclusion.
It is not necessary that before reversing a judgment of acquittal, an appellate court must characterize the findings of the lower court as perverse.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: Section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not bar the trial of an accused for a distinct offence, such as one under Section 353 of the Indian Penal Code, even if it is based on the same set of facts as an offence under Section 186 of the Indian Penal Code, because the two offences have different ingredients and quality. Furthermore, an appellate court has the full and undoubted power to review the entire evidence in an appeal against acquittal and come to its own conclusion, and is not constrained by rigid formulas like 'substantial and compelling reasons' or the need to find the trial court's findings perverse.
legal_tests_applied: Section 195 of the Criminal Procedure Code does not bar the trial of an accused person for a distinct offence disclosed by the same set of facts, but which is not within the ambit of that section.

The test suggested by the expression 'substantial and compelling reasons' for reversing a judgment of acquittal, should not be construed as a formula which has to be rigidly applied in every case, and it is not necessary that before reversing a judgment of acquittal, the High Court must necessarily characterise the findings recorded therein as perverse.

An appellate Court in an appeal against acquittal has the power to review the entire evidence and to come to its own conclusion, but in doing so should not only consider every matter on record having a bearing on the questions of fact and the reasons given by the Court below in support of its order of acquittal, but should express the reasons in its judgment, which led it to hold that the acquittal was not justified.
why_appellant_lost: The argument that the conviction under Section 353 IPC was a circumvention of Section 195 CrPC was rejected because Sections 186 and 353 IPC are two distinct offences with different ingredients and quality; Section 186 deals with obstruction of a public servant, while Section 353 requires the additional ingredient of assault or use of criminal force.

The contention that the High Court was not justified in interfering with the acquittal was rejected because the High Court correctly exercised its wide appellate power to review the entire evidence, relying on the testimony of multiple witnesses (P.Ws 1, 2, 3 and 9 to 13) to conclude that the appellants used criminal force against public servants in the performance of their duties.
why_respondent_won: The prosecution under Section 353 IPC was valid because it is a distinct offence from Section 186 IPC, and the bar under Section 195 CrPC does not apply to distinct offences even if they arise from the same facts.

The High Court's interference with the acquittal was justified because an appellate court's power in an appeal against acquittal is as wide as its power in an appeal against conviction, allowing it to review all evidence and reach its own conclusion after considering the trial court's reasoning.
